sysd-reliab-121.title: Rainbow tables: cracking hashes by lookup
sysd-reliab-121.text: A rainbow table is a bargain struck between storage and processing time. It is a precomputed table of cryptographic hash outputs, usually used to recover passwords from stolen hashes. It needs less processing time and more storage than brute force, and more processing time and less storage than a table holding the hash of every possible password. It stores only the ends of long chains built by alternating the hash function with reduction functions. A table fits one hash function and fails against large salts, which would need a table per salt value. Use declined as of 2020, as salting spread and GPU brute force became practical.

sysd-reliab-020.title: Salted password hashing: how to store a password
sysd-reliab-020.text:
Store a password as plain text, and anyone with internal access can read it. Store a bare hash, and precomputation attacks such as rainbow tables can undo it. The safer practice is to store each password as a hash of the password plus a unique random salt, never as plain text or a bare hash.

According to OWASP, a salt is a unique, randomly generated string added to each password as part of the hashing process. It is not meant to be secret and can be stored in plain text in the database. What it does is make the hash result unique to each password. The database stores the hash of the password plus the salt.

To validate a login, the system fetches the user's salt, appends it to the entered password, hashes the result, and compares it with the stored hash. If they match, the password is valid.

sysd-reliab-136.title: OAuth 2.0 clients and endpoints
sysd-reliab-136.text: Before OAuth does anything, the client has to introduce itself. It registers with the authorization server, giving its client type and redirection URIs, and the server issues a unique client identifier. That identifier is not a secret and must not alone authenticate the client. A confidential client can keep its credentials secret, for example on a secure server. A public client cannot, as with an installed native application or a browser-based one. Three endpoints do the work. The authorization endpoint obtains authorization by redirecting the user-agent (the browser), the token endpoint exchanges a grant for an access token, and the client's redirection endpoint receives responses.

sysd-reliab-023.title: The OAuth 2.0 flow, from request to resource
sysd-reliab-023.text:
The whole of OAuth 2.0 comes down to one exchange: the client asks for a token, and the resource server accepts it. In this flow a client obtains an access token from the authorization server, with the resource owner's consent, and uses it to request resources from the resource server.

First the client requests authorization from the authorization server. It supplies its client id and secret as identification, the scopes it wants, and an endpoint URI to receive the access token or authorization code. The authorization server authenticates the client and verifies that the requested scopes are permitted, and the resource owner interacts with it to grant access. The server then redirects back to the client with an authorization code or an access token, depending on the grant type. It may also return a refresh token.

With the access token the client asks the resource server for the resource. The resource server accepts and validates the token and returns the appropriate resources. The way the token is obtained is called an authorization grant, or authorization flow. The framework specifies several grant types for different use cases, such as Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC), which {{ref:sysd-reliab-132}} compares.

sysd-reliab-132.title: OAuth 2.0 grant types compared
sysd-reliab-132.text:
A grant is how a client proves it has permission to ask for a token. An authorization grant is a credential representing the resource owner's authorization that the client uses to obtain an access token. RFC 6749 defines four grant types and a way to add more.

The first type sends the resource owner to the authorization server, which authenticates them and returns an authorization code. The owner's credentials are never shared with the client. The code lets the server authenticate the client and delivers the access token directly to the client, without passing through the user-agent, where it could be exposed. This grant is optimized for confidential clients, and {{ref:sysd-reliab-133}} walks through it.

The implicit grant, for in-browser JavaScript clients, issues an access token directly, with no intermediate code, and saves round trips. But it does not authenticate the client, it exposes the token to the user-agent, and it issues no refresh token.

The resource owner password credentials grant exchanges the user's own username and password for a token. Use it only where the client is highly trusted, such as the device operating system, and no other grant is available. It carries higher risk because it keeps the password anti-pattern the protocol avoids: the client could abuse or leak the password. In the client credentials grant, the client authenticates with only its own credentials, when acting on its own behalf or on access previously arranged. Only confidential clients may use it, and it should not include a refresh token. Extension grants use an absolute URI, defined by the authorization server, as the grant_type value.

sysd-reliab-133.title: The authorization code grant, step by step
sysd-reliab-133.text:
The authorization code grant is a redirection-based flow that obtains access and refresh tokens via the user-agent and is optimized for confidential clients. Its trick is a two-step exchange: the browser carries only a short-lived code, and the real token goes straight to the client.

The client directs the user-agent to the authorization endpoint with its client identifier, requested scope, local state and a redirection URI. The server authenticates the resource owner and establishes whether they grant or deny access. If access is granted, the server redirects the user-agent to the redirection URI with an authorization code and any state the client provided. The client then makes a POST to the token endpoint with grant_type authorization_code, authenticating and repeating the redirection URI. The server authenticates the client, validates the code, checks that the URI matches, and returns an access token and optionally a refresh token.

Several safeguards surround the code. It must expire shortly after it is issued, with a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes recommended, and the client must not use it more than once. If a code is used twice, the server must deny the request and should revoke tokens previously issued from it. The code is bound to the client identifier and redirection URI. The recommended state parameter, which the server returns unchanged, helps prevent cross-site request forgery. If the redirection URI is missing, invalid or mismatching, the server must not automatically redirect the user-agent to it.

sysd-reliab-035.title: Attacks on OAuth 2.0 and their defenses
sysd-reliab-035.text:
OAuth moves secrets through browsers and redirects, and attackers have found the weak spots. If an attacker alters redirect_uri, the authorization code can reach a URI they control. The server must check that the URI used to get the code matches the one used to redeem it. An open redirector forwards a user-agent to any location named in a parameter. It can leak a code or token if clients may register only part of a redirection URI. CSRF against a client's redirection URI lets an attacker inject their own code, so the client needs a non-guessable state parameter.

In clickjacking, an attacker loads the authorization page in a transparent iframe over dummy buttons, and servers can send an x-frame-options header of deny or sameorigin. Secrets must never travel in the clear, so the server must require TLS on its endpoints. A formal analysis also found the AS Mix-Up Attack, in which a client forwards secrets to a malicious one of several authorization servers. The draft of OAuth 2.1 recommends PKCE for all types of client; {{ref:sysd-reliab-137}} explains it.

sysd-reliab-137.title: PKCE: a one-time secret for the authorization code
sysd-reliab-137.text:
On a phone, a malicious app can register as a handler for the legitimate app's custom URI scheme and receive its authorization code. A secret built into the client would not stop it. Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is an OAuth 2.0 extension that binds the code to a one-time secret only the real client holds.

For each authorization request the client creates a random secret, the code verifier, and sends a code challenge derived from it. Later it sends the code with the verifier, and the server transforms the verifier, compares it with the stored challenge, and denies access if they differ. The verifier never crossed a channel the attacker can observe, so an intercepted code is useless.

The verifier is a high-entropy random string of 43 to 128 characters. The challenge is either the verifier itself, called plain, which an eavesdropper can see, or S256, the base64url encoding of the SHA-256 hash of the verifier. A client that can use S256 must, and it must never downgrade to plain afterward.

sysd-reliab-128.title: Preventing XSS: encode, sanitize, restrict
sysd-reliab-128.text: Stopping XSS starts with how output is written. Contextual output encoding escapes untrusted strings for where they land in the document: HTML entity, JavaScript, CSS or URL escaping. Apps that need no rich input can largely eliminate XSS this way. When users may submit HTML, encoding is not enough, because the browser must render it. A sanitization engine then lets safe elements through and escapes dangerous ones such as script tags. Session cookies are a target because client-side scripts can read them. An HttpOnly flag makes a cookie unavailable to scripts, and SameSite=Strict strips it from cross-origin requests, though neither fully prevents XSS.

sysd-reliab-124.title: WebAuthn: logging in with a key pair instead of a password
sysd-reliab-124.text:
Passwords fail in familiar ways: people reuse them across services, choose weak ones, and sites store them badly. WebAuthn is a W3C web standard defining an API that websites use to authenticate users with public-key credentials, commonly called passkeys. It verifies identity with digital signatures instead of shared passwords. An authenticator, a device or program, proves to the website that the user possesses it. At registration, its signed attestation statement carries the public key the website later uses to verify its signed assertions.

Platform authenticators are built into the operating system, such as Windows Hello and Apple Keychain. Roaming ones connect over USB, Bluetooth Low Energy or NFC. The scheme resists some phishing, the luring of users to fake sites, because the authenticator only offers credentials registered on the same website. A roaming hardware authenticator resists malware, because its keys sit on a separate device. WebAuthn grew from U2F, which improved on TOTP and SMS codes that left users open to phishing. Although touted as a password replacement, most sites implementing it still use passwords in some capacity.

sysd-reliab-029.title: API security practices
sysd-reliab-029.text:
Securing an API comes down to a short list. One guide's tips are to use OAuth2, WebAuthn and leveled API keys. Then add authorization, rate limiting, whitelisting, an API gateway, error handling, input validation and API versioning, and check the OWASP API security risks.

Several of these build on earlier entries. With OAuth 2.0, an access token replaces the user's password. The resource server understands it, and it can carry fewer rights than the grant that produced it. Tokens go only over TLS, never in the clear. WebAuthn verifies identity with digital signatures. Authorization should follow least privilege, so every module, user or program can access only what its legitimate purpose needs.

Two tips guard against abuse. Input validation guards against code injection, where unsanitized input modifies application logic. Rate limiting matters for credentials. Without it, an attacker can try an arbitrary number of codes until one works. A limit tied to a session ID can be reset by creating new sessions.

sysd-reliab-131.title: Zero trust: no one is trusted by default
sysd-reliab-131.text:
Sitting inside the corporate network is not reason enough to be trusted. Zero trust is a security strategy in which users and devices are not trusted by default. That holds even on a privileged network such as a corporate LAN, and even for users and devices verified before. Trust based on a perimeter or a VPN is commonly not enough for networks of many zones, cloud services, remote and mobile environments and IoT devices.

Instead, zero trust establishes identity verification, validates device compliance before granting access, and ensures least privilege access to only explicitly authorized resources. It advocates mutual authentication that checks the identity and integrity of users and devices regardless of location. NIST SP 800-207 defines it as concepts that reduce the uncertainty of enforcing accurate per-request access decisions when the network is viewed as compromised. A full solution includes enhanced identity governance with policy-based access controls, micro-segmentation, and overlay networks or software-defined perimeters.

sysd-reliab-140.title: Signed, encrypted and nested JWTs
sysd-reliab-140.text: A JWT can be signed, encrypted, both, or neither. It is carried either as a signed JWS or an encrypted JWE, may nest one inside the other, and can also be left unsecured. In a JWS the claims are digitally signed and form the payload. In a JWE they are the encrypted plaintext. When both are needed, producers should normally sign first and then encrypt, which prevents stripping the signature and gives the signer privacy. An unsecured JWT is a JWS with the alg value none and an empty signature. A conforming implementation must support only HS256 and none, while RS256 and ES256 are recommended.

sysd-reliab-033.title: JWT security pitfalls
sysd-reliab-033.text:
The worst JWT mistake is letting the token say how it should be checked. Some JWT libraries validated tokens wrongly based on the alg field, most commonly by accepting alg=none. Developers should never let the JWT header alone drive verification. Even a token that validates should be rejected unless its algorithms are acceptable, which is an application decision. A token's contents also cannot be trusted unless they are cryptographically secured and the signing key is verifiably under the issuer's control.

Storage and privacy matter too. A JWT should reach the client by a secure mechanism such as an HTTP-only cookie, because client-side JavaScript can read local or session storage. A JWT may carry privacy-sensitive information, so encrypt it or send it only over TLS.

The deepest trade-off is statelessness. If a service must invalidate a session before the token expires, it can no longer trust the token alone and must check a data store. That removes the main advantage of JWTs. Some have argued that JWTs are hard to use securely because the standard offers many algorithms and options.

sysd-reliab-123.title: Argon2: a password hash that costs memory
sysd-reliab-123.text: Argon2 is a key derivation function that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition. It makes brute-force attacks expensive by using a large, fixed-size memory region. All three modes are tuned by execution time, memory required and degree of parallelism. Argon2d maximizes resistance to GPU cracking but risks side-channel attacks, Argon2i resists those, and Argon2id is a hybrid. RFC 9106 recommends Argon2id if you do not know the difference or if side-channel attacks are a viable threat. Its default for all environments is 2 GiB of memory, 1 iteration and parallelism 4. Where memory is constrained, it suggests 64 MiB, 3 iterations and parallelism 4.

sysd-reliab-122.title: bcrypt: a hash that can be made slower
sysd-reliab-122.text: bcrypt is a password-hashing function, based on the Blowfish cipher, designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières. It incorporates a salt against rainbow table attacks. It is also adaptive: the iteration count can be raised over time, so it stays resistant to brute-force search as computing power grows. Its key setup repeats a configurable number of rekeying rounds, which can make hashing arbitrarily slow. Inputs are a password of up to 72 bytes, a cost and a 16-byte salt. The cost is log2 of the iterations, so 12 means 4,096. Passwords are cut at 72 bytes, only 18 characters in the worst case of 4-byte UTF-8.

sysd-reliab-119.title: How attackers get around MFA
sysd-reliab-119.text: MFA raises the bar, but it can still be bypassed through phishing, SIM swapping, fatigue attacks and implementation flaws. Many approaches remain vulnerable to phishing, man-in-the-browser and man-in-the-middle attacks, so users should not share verification codes with anyone. SMS codes are weak. Phones can be cloned, and maintenance personnel can read texts. SS7 vulnerabilities let messages be redirected to attackers, and SIM swap attacks hand duplicate SIM cards to criminals. An MFA fatigue attack floods a user with push login requests until one is accepted by mistake. Number matching is an interim mitigation, and phishing-resistant MFA is advised instead of push notifications.

sysd-reliab-026.title: Identity provider
sysd-reliab-026.text: Somebody has to keep the list of who the users are. An identity provider is a centralized trusted system that stores and manages user identities and authenticates users on behalf of other applications. It authenticates a user either by validating a username and password or by validating an assertion from a separate identity provider. Service providers rely on it to assert who a user is. A service provider may still keep a local account for the user, holding attributes unique to its own service. An identity broker connects many service providers with different identity providers, so one login works with any application, whatever protocol it follows.

sysd-reliab-025.title: Single sign-on: log in once, reach everything
sysd-reliab-025.text:
Single sign-on is an authentication scheme in which a user logs in once, with a single set of credentials, to reach several related but independent applications. It removes the need to log in separately to each application, and true single sign-on lets the user access services without re-entering authentication factors. It works because credentials and identity information are kept in one place, by the central trusted system that {{ref:sysd-reliab-026}} describes.

In the flow, the user requests a resource and the application redirects them to the identity provider. The user signs in, the identity provider sends a single sign-on response to the application, and the application grants access. Same sign-on is different: every application still asks for authentication but reuses credentials from a directory server, where true single sign-on passes one authentication token. Because applications support different authentication mechanisms, it must store the credentials used at first sign-in and translate them for each system. The converse, single log-out, ends access to several systems with one action.

Benefits include one set of credentials to remember, less password fatigue and lower IT support cost.

sysd-reliab-125.title: Kerberos: tickets instead of passwords on the wire
sysd-reliab-125.text:
On a network where anyone can listen, Kerberos never sends your password. It is a ticket-based protocol for proving identity on a non-secure network, with mutual authentication: user and server each verify the other. It builds on symmetric-key cryptography and needs a trusted third party, the key distribution center (KDC), whose authentication server (AS) and ticket-granting service (TGS) issue the tickets.

At logon the client authenticates to the AS, which returns a time-stamped ticket-granting ticket (TGT) encrypted with the TGS's secret key. To use a service, the client sends the TGT to the TGS, which issues a service ticket and session keys. The client presents that ticket to the service, which decrypts it with its own secret key and checks the client's authenticator. It replies with the timestamp encrypted under the session key, which lets the client trust the server.

Tickets have a lifetime, so clocks must be synchronized within configured limits, five minutes by default in MIT's setup, or authentication fails. A central KDC is also a weak point: compromising it lets an attacker impersonate any user.

sysd-reliab-036.title: OpenID: sign in through a third-party provider
sysd-reliab-036.text: OpenID is an open, decentralized authentication protocol that lets users sign in to many sites through a third-party identity provider. A site, the relying party, uses that provider to authenticate users. It needs no login system of its own, and users need no separate password for each site. The provider gives each user a unique identifier, an OpenID, and prompts them to authenticate when a supporting site redirects them there. The design has weak spots. A malicious relying party can send users to a bogus provider page to steal credentials, and the provider's log of every OpenID login makes cross-site tracking easier.

sysd-reliab-037.title: The risks of single sign-on
sysd-reliab-037.text:
Single sign-on trades convenience for a bigger target. Because one login unlocks many resources, stolen credentials do more damage, and a compromised main SSO password exposes every supported application. It should ideally be paired with strong methods such as smart cards and one-time password tokens. It also increases dependence on highly available authentication systems. Losing them can deny access to every system unified under it, though session failover can keep operation going. Where access must be guaranteed at all times, as in security or plant-floor systems, that risk may make single sign-on undesirable.

Authentication is also slower, because every application must ask the SSO provider to verify. The SSO token cannot be protected with the HttpOnly cookie flag. An XSS flaw on the logged-out website can let an attacker steal it and hijack the session. A stolen SSO session reaches every site using the system. Kerberos and the XML-based scheme in {{ref:sysd-reliab-027}} originally gave users no choice about releasing personal information. As federated services spread and privacy rules such as the GDPR tighten, {{ref:sysd-reliab-024}} has become more attractive.

sysd-reliab-027.title: SAML: identity assertions in XML
sysd-reliab-027.text: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an open XML-based standard for sharing identity, authentication and permission information between systems, such as an identity provider and a service provider. It enables identity federation: identity providers securely pass authenticated identities and their attributes to service providers. In single sign-on, the user requests a resource at a service provider. It sends an authentication request to the identity provider through the user's browser and trusts the identity information it gets back. SAML is geared to enterprise security but can be complex to install and maintain. OAuth and OIDC use JSON and RESTful communication that suit mobile and modern web applications.

sysd-reliab-038.title: Single sign-on configurations
sysd-reliab-038.text: Single sign-on can ride on different mechanisms. In the Kerberos setup, the initial sign-on gets a ticket-granting ticket. Other applications, such as email clients, wikis and revision-control systems, use it to acquire service tickets without another prompt. In the smart-card setup, the initial sign-on prompts for the card, and other applications use it too, with certificates or passwords stored on it. Mobile devices can log users onto many systems using OpenID Connect or SAML with an X.509 certificate identifying the device, which counts as something you have.
